# Numerical Methods for Physicists

A course on how a physicist solves problems that have no analytic solution. One lecture is one physical problem: the pendulum and chaos, a chain of oscillators, electrostatics, heat conduction, waves, quantum mechanics, cosmology, hydrodynamics, radiative transfer. The methods needed (eigenproblems, sparse systems, the FFT, spherical harmonics, the SVD) are introduced when a problem cannot be solved without them. The language is Python with Numba.

## Course lectures

::: {.lecture-accordion}


<p class="course-kicker">Preparation</p>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">01</span><span>Python, NumPy and Numba</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The working environment (a virtual environment, Jupyter and Quarto), Python basics, NumPy arrays and vectorization, Matplotlib plots, timing, compiling critical loops with Numba.

**Tools:** a virtual environment, Jupyter, NumPy arrays, slicing and broadcasting, data types and precision, a seeded random number generator, Matplotlib, `%timeit`, Numba (`@njit`: when it helps and when it does not).

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>

<p class="course-kicker">Part I. Motion and oscillations</p>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">02</span><span>The pendulum: how a numerical method goes wrong</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

From Euler to Runge–Kutta and Verlet: order of accuracy, local and global error, stability, energy conservation, the convergence test.

**Tools:** floating-point numbers and machine precision, order of a method, the convergence test, the Euler, Runge–Kutta and Verlet schemes, symplecticity.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">03</span><span>Chaos: the double pendulum and the three-body problem</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

Adaptive step size and error control, the Lyapunov exponent, Poincaré sections. Why an «exact» numerical solution of a chaotic system is impossible and what then counts as a result.

**Tools:** adaptive Runge–Kutta methods (solve_ivp), the Lyapunov exponent, the Poincaré section, ensembles of trajectories and Numba acceleration.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">04</span><span>Coupled oscillators and normal modes</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

A chain of $N$ masses: the stiffness matrix, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, the dispersion relation. The limit $N\to\infty$ gives the wave equation.

**Tools:** a matrix as an operator, eigenproblems (eigh), tridiagonal matrices, the condition number.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>

<p class="course-kicker">Part II. Fields, diffusion and waves</p>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">05</span><span>Electrostatics: the Poisson equation and large linear systems</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

A finite-difference scheme turns the equation into a linear system with $N^2$ unknowns. Direct (LU, Cholesky) and iterative (Jacobi, Seidel, conjugate gradients) methods; what accuracy costs.

**Tools:** sparse matrices, LU and Cholesky, Jacobi, Seidel and conjugate-gradient iterations, the condition number, the idea of the multigrid method.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">06</span><span>Heat conduction and diffusion</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The explicit scheme and its stability condition, the implicit scheme and tridiagonal solver, Crank–Nicolson. Comparison with the Green function; inhomogeneous and nonlinear media; the random walk as the microscopic picture.

**Tools:** von Neumann stability analysis, implicit schemes, the tridiagonal (Thomas) algorithm, the method of lines, stiff systems.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">07</span><span>Waves and the telegraph equation</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The wave equation, the CFL condition, numerical dispersion and dissipation; upwind, Lax–Wendroff and leapfrog schemes. The telegraph equation as a bridge between waves and diffusion.

**Tools:** the method of characteristics, the CFL condition, numerical dispersion, absorbing boundary conditions.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">08</span><span>Fourier analysis: frequencies in a signal and spectral solution of equations</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The DFT and FFT, aliasing, spectral leakage and windows, the convolution theorem, spectral differentiation and exponential accuracy, the Gibbs phenomenon.

**Tools:** the FFT, windows, convolution via the FFT, spectral derivatives, dealiasing.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>

<p class="course-kicker">Part III. Quantum mechanics</p>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">09</span><span>The Schrödinger equation: energy levels</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The Hamiltonian as a matrix (finite differences and a basis), shooting and the Numerov method, convergence of levels, the variational principle.

**Tools:** diagonalization of tridiagonal matrices, shooting and root finding, the Numerov method, convergence of levels.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">10</span><span>Quantum evolution: wave packets, tunnelling, neutrino oscillations</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

Crank–Nicolson (unitarity), operator splitting (split-step) with the FFT, the matrix exponential and expansion in eigenvectors, adiabaticity.

**Tools:** split-step Fourier, the matrix exponential (expm), unitarity as a test, the adiabatic limit.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>

<p class="course-kicker">Part IV. The Universe and data</p>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">11</span><span>Cosmology: the expansion of the Universe and «freeze-out»</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

Only a minimum of cosmology is needed: Hubble's law and the Friedmann equation, which reads as energy conservation (by analogy with lectures 2–3). The age of the Universe and distances through quadratures, root finding, fitting the Hubble diagram. A simple stiff problem: relaxation to equilibrium that the expansion «freezes» — explicit and implicit methods.

**Tools:** numerical integration (rectangles, trapezoids, Simpson, Gauss) and the order of convergence, root finding (bisection, Newton), `curve_fit`, stiffness and the implicit Euler method.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">12</span><span>Functions on the sphere: multipoles and sky maps</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

Legendre polynomials and spherical harmonics, the addition theorem, Gauss–Legendre quadrature in $\cos\theta$, expansion of a map on a sphere and the power spectrum $C_\ell$. Gauss nodes as an eigenvalue problem (lecture 4).

**Tools:** $Y_{\ell m}$, Gauss–Legendre quadrature, stability of recurrence relations, analysis and synthesis of a map.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">13</span><span>Inverse problems: the reactor antineutrino spectrum and the SVD</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The singular value decomposition, the condition number, the pseudo-inverse, truncated SVD and Tikhonov regularization, best low-rank approximation. Convolution with the detector resolution and its inversion through the FFT (lecture 8).

**Tools:** the SVD, the pseudo-inverse, regularization, low rank; the Cholesky factorization for generating correlated errors (link to the statistics course).

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>

<p class="course-kicker">Part V. Flows, transport and large computations</p>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">14</span><span>Hydrodynamics I: conservation laws and shock waves</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

Conservative form, the finite-volume method, Lax–Friedrichs and Godunov fluxes, numerical viscosity, flux limiters (TVD), the CFL condition.

**Tools:** conservative schemes, finite volumes, the Riemann problem, flux limiters.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">15</span><span>Hydrodynamics II: vortices and two-dimensional turbulence</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The vorticity equation and the stream function, solving the Poisson equation with the FFT, the pseudo-spectral method and dealiasing, the Reynolds number and grid resolution, acceleration with Numba.

**Tools:** the pseudo-spectral method, the 2/3 rule, time integration, reuse of the Poisson solver and FFT from lectures 5 and 8.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">16</span><span>The transport equation: from Boltzmann to light in water</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The collision integral, the mean free path, the transport problem. Methods: Monte Carlo (the random walk of a photon), the diffusion approximation, expansion in angular moments (lecture 12). Comparison of cost and accuracy.

**Tools:** Monte Carlo for transport (sampling free paths and angles), the $1/\sqrt N$ error, the diffusion approximation, $P_N$.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">17</span><span>Fast computations and verification: from a prototype to production code</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

Profiling, vectorization and Numba, reuse of computations (caching, low rank from lecture 13), tests on analytic limits, the method of manufactured solutions, error budgets.

**Tools:** profiling, Numba (njit, parallel, the risks of fastmath), caching, regression and convergence tests.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
